title: BBC lodges urgent appeal against Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit
summary:
Corporation asks US court of appeals for the 11th circuit to throw out case brought over Panorama documentary

The BBC has lodged an urgent appeal to have Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation…

blocks.text: The BBC has lodged an urgent appeal to have Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against it thrown out, after internal surprise at a judge’s decision to allow the case to go to trial.
The corporation is currently heading to court next year over a Panorama documentary that spliced together two parts of Trump’s speech made before the 6 January insurrection at the US Capitol.

While the broadcaster has apologised over the edit, which featured in the 2024 programme Trump: A Second Chance, it has always denied that the film defamed Trump. It has also said it was never broadcast in Florida, where Trump’s legal action is being heard.

The federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz, a Trump appointee, ruled earlier this month that the lawsuit could proceed, denying the BBC’s attempt to have the case thrown out. However, the BBC has now appealed to a higher court, the United States court of appeals for the 11th circuit, restating that the Florida court has no jurisdiction to hear the case.

In a legal submission seen by the Guardian, the BBC’s lawyers state that the documentary “never aired in the United States”. It argues that Kuntz found the Florida court held jurisdiction over the BBC “despite the complete lack of evidence that anyone accessed it there, as both Florida law and this circuit’s precedent require”.

The move is a sign of the BBC’s desperation to have the case dismissed, given the time, expense and political headache it is causing, while it is also making huge cuts at home and holding talks with the UK government over its future funding.

“We are surprised and disappointed by the court’s decision that this case should be heard in Florida,” said a BBC spokesperson. “As we have made clear from the start, the BBC broadcast this documentary in the UK – and UK only. We did not show it in Florida, nor did any other broadcaster.
“Given the urgency of this issue, we are now requesting a higher court review the ruling.”
The spliced clip suggested that Trump told a crowd: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol and I’ll be there with you, and we fight. We fight like hell.”
The words were taken from sections of his speech almost an hour apart.

Kuntz was nominated to his current role by Trump and confirmed by a Senate vote earlier this year, which split down party lines, Republicans in favour, with Democrat and independent senators voting against the appointment. Three senators did not vote.

Kuntz ruled earlier this month that Trump had sufficiently pleaded “actual malice” on behalf of the BBC’s editing. “Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm,” he wrote.
On his Truth Social site, Trump described the ruling as a “huge victory against fake news BBC”.

In its appeal, the BBC’s legal team states that the Florida court “ignored the BBC’s rigorous and systematic efforts to prevent access to the documentary and its other streaming content in the United States”.

“This erroneous exercise of jurisdiction over the BBC is anathema to the due process requirements of personal jurisdiction and to the comity interests in allowing other sovereign nations to police their own affairs,” it states.

“The BBC did not produce, film, or air the documentary in Florida. Rather, the BBC aired it on its UK TV channels, and also made it available on the UK iPlayer streaming service. The BBC never broadcast it in the US, nor did it have the rights to do so. Third parties acquired the international distribution rights … though they never aired it in the US.”
Trump himself is still due to give a deposition in the case, a process in which he is questioned by lawyers under oath. However, it has been postponed until January.
